doc.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

chapter: Race, education and the future of jazz
title: Race and her own experience
summary: Asked about reverse prejudice, she says she never felt it; mentions Gus Johnson, Maxine Sullivan and John Hammond's praise.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Over the years, did you ever run into any racial — I don’t know exactly what the word would be—

I suppose you know I’ve only been blonde for a few years since I started to go gray. I used to be very, very dark. In fact when Gus Johnson met me for the first time he believed that I was black. And I have very dark skin. And I don’t know whether, I don’t think people feel any different regardless of what color they are. I think that there has

been times when I’ve read articles about people not liking a singer because they were of a different colored persuasion you know? But it’s never actually happened to me. I don’t believe so. I’ve worked with performers and I roomed with Maxine Sullivan and I never felt it, and I don’t think anyone ever made me feel conscious of it. The fact that John Hammond — Hank O’Neil once said “you’re the only singer that John Hammond ever said anything nice about except for the ones that he really loved, Billie and Bessie.” He said to Hank, “Have you heard this girl, Pug Horton?” And Hank said, “No I haven’t.” He said, “She’s all right” which I thought was a very high compliment. And of course I worked with musicians of all color. I mean it didn’t bother me so why would it bother them? I mean my heart was in the right place.
